    von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

    Industry observers note that brBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe. The match ended 3–0, sparking immense hype around Brighton’s pressing. This analysis explores the underlying mechanisms: their man-oriented pressing across the entire pitch, their asymmetrical build-up play, their transition behavior after winning the ball, and the three goals themselves.

    Arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession. Any opponent who sets out to establish order is playing on the ground Arsenal own. Hürzeler therefore decided against control – not control surrendered in the sense of a low block, but a chaotic game state that Brighton generated themselves and were therefore prepared for.

    System & movement with the ball – FC Arsenal.

    System & movement with the ball – Brighton & Hove Albion.

    According to recent reports, the thread running through ninety minutes: Arsenal were not to settle into an organised phase either with or without the ball. Three decisions delivered that. The build-up was set up asymmetrically – on the right Brighton prepared the long ball and occupied the landing zone before it was played, on the left counter-movements opened the short route. It was never long instead of short, but two prepared options that would have demanded opposite answers from Arsenal. After regains the ball was not secured but risked immediately, because a secured ball gives the opponent exactly the seconds they need to reorganise. And the press lived off intensity and constantly latest starting points: when a line was played through, Brighton did not stand still but re-established their shape and triggered again.

    Sources indicate that all three decisions give up ball control in the classical sense. Control came instead from preparation – if you know where the ball will land and you are standing there beforehand, you control the situation without the ball.

    Recent findings suggest that what followed can be pinned to a single number: 41 Arsenal turnovers in their own danger zone. That is not a figure a side of this quality produces because they play badly, but because they never reached the game state their build-up is designed for.

    Brightons manorientated press against a 4-3-3.

    The press was simple in principle and demanding in execution. Brighton set up with man-reference to their direct opponent and switched into pure man-marking on the trigger. Against a side that tracks from the first second, marking assignments can be pulled apart by movement before any pressure exists; Brighton refused to offer that, because their shape stayed compact until the trigger moment.

    In the “mid-block,” positioned +1 on the last line, but ready at any moment to transition into a high press upon a pressing trigger.

    It has been revealed that the steering began with Ayari. He curved his pressing run so that Konsa stayed in his cover shadow and Raya was forced to the other side. Kostoulas marked Gabriel, while Chema Andrés and Groß pushed aggressively onto Arsenal’s No. 8s. Groß in particular tracked the dropping Rice and at times advanced into the first pressing line, in some sequences all the way onto Konsa. That requires Rice to be picked up by a team-mate in the same moment – the man-marking worked through handovers as much as through tracking. Centrally, the striker and the No. 10 rotated accordingly: whoever had the shorter route to the next man on the ball pushed out, while the other covered behind him and took over again on the next trigger.

    It only held up because the centre-backs came with it. Vušković and Struijk stepped out onto Ødegaard and the dropping Havertz and prevented an underload in central areas. When Arsenal built with three in the first line, Brighton kept one centre-back zonal in the back line – but with permanent reference to the unmarked player in the No. 6 space, stepping onto him the moment the press was triggered. Arsenal’s numerical advantage in build-up therefore never translated into a free man anywhere on the pitch.

    Raya was part of the marking scheme too. Ayari’s cover shadow left only the route through a No. 6, and under man-marking that is not an escape but a duel that begins with the first touch. Raya’s body shape reinforced it: he tended to open only half-way, which effectively removed the switch to the far side from his repertoire. Steered onto his right foot, only the right-hand build-up side remained; the left lay open for long stretches and was unreachable for the one player who could have found it.

    Every back pass served as a trigger. When the ball went back to Raya or the centre-backs, Brighton pushed up as a unit and raised the defensive line. The density around the ball came less from the base shape than from the recovery runs: players who had been beaten sprinted back, and they did not run at the ball but with a cover shadow onto the lay-off option behind it. An Arsenal player with a marker in his back therefore had neither the lay-off nor the chance to turn.

    This is precisely where Brighton differed from most sides who get played through against Arsenal. The usual response is to stay deep once a line has been broken and wait for the shape to settle. Brighton instead pushed up into the next line and used the mid-block to prepare the next jump back into the high press – even when that press had just been beaten. The press therefore had not one starting point per possession, but a steady supply of fresh ones, and Arsenal had to solve the same pressure several times within a single attack.

    Arsenal’s core problem was the absence of a threat in behind. Their attempts to play through the press came without pace beyond the back line, so Brighton were never forced to turn towards their own goal. That made the press cheap: no threat in behind, therefore no need to drop the line. There are three answers to committed man-marking – movement that drags your own marker away and opens space for a third player, a dribble that beats the assignment one-on-one, or a target man who wins the long balls. Arsenal produced none of them.

    Industry observers note that when the high press was beaten, Brighton dropped into a 5-1-4 and inverted the priority. The five in the last line formed a deliberate overload against Arsenal’s front line – in exactly the moment a man-oriented side is most vulnerable, because its players are facing forward while the opponents are already moving. Brighton took the depth out of the situation first and only then thought about the ball again.

    A “mid-block” in a 5-1-4 formation. The foremost players protected the “red zone” by using their cover shadows and shifting extremely compactly. Arsenal was mostly forced to play around the block, repeatedly giving Brighton time to reorganize.

    According to recent reports, A single No. 6 held the connection in front, while the four most advanced players stayed narrow and closed the centre with cover shadows rather than pressing the ball carrier. Arsenal found no central switch on the ball-near side and had to play around the block. Every trip around it cost seconds that Brighton used to shift across, so the end of the route offered the same congestion as the start. In some phases six players stood in the last line.

    The block was not a terminus. At every Arsenal back pass Brighton jumped out again and restarted the high press – the same trigger as in the high phase, only from a deeper starting position. The spare man in the last line made that possible, usually Vušković: because the overload left him without a fixed opponent, he could step out, cover the depth and pick up a man himself a moment later. That freed a midfielder to push forward without leaving an assignment open behind him – precisely the point at which sides with a similar approach usually come apart.

    In the “mid-block” phase, the “+1” players organized themselves to execute early handovers and jump into pressing situations. Here, Vuskovic—acting as the “+1” player from the defensive line—steps up to pick up the Arsenal player operating in the number 10 position.

    On top of that came the trap on the touchline. Once Brighton steered the ball wide, players jumped in from every direction: the ball-near winger closed the route back, the No. 6 covered inside, the back line stepped out. The back pass, the switch and the ball in behind did not disappear one after another but at the same time. Take away only the back pass and a side switches play; take away only the switch and they play backwards and start again. When all that remains is an individual action against several opponents with the touchline at your back, it almost always ends with the opposition.

    Sources indicate that after a regain there are two basic options: risk the ball immediately to launch the attack, or secure it to establish order. Hürzeler consistently chose the first, and it follows directly from the overall idea – a secured ball would have given Arsenal exactly the seconds in which their structure reorganises.

    When a high press was bypassed, Brighton succeeded in forcing Arsenal into congested situations in the area in front of the back four. In doing so, the players who had been bypassed shifted to block the passing lanes of the players positioned behind the ball. This created additional pressure on the ball carrier, who was simultaneously facing pressure from the front via a “negative” pressing movement (i.e., pressing towards their own goal).

    The counter was prepared before the regain. When Arsenal found a player in the No. 6 space after beating the press, Brighton immediately closed his back pass, so the turnover inevitably occurred in a moment when Arsenal were all ahead of the ball. The density around the ball, a defensive necessity, meant in attack that Brighton were central and therefore on the shortest route to goal. The first ball went to the deepest player, followed by a dribble at speed into the box, with no intermediate step and no square pass for safety.

    Sources indicate that in the build-up phase, Brighton utilized a diamond shape. De Cuyper and Boscagli engaged in a 2v2 duel on the left flank, while Kostoulas, Gomez, and Kadioglu created a high 3v3 situation on the right. Briefly, both center-backs and a defensive midfielder would spread out to widen the formation. Additional support occasionally came from Groß, dropping back from the number 10 position. Ayari occupied Konsa and Gabriel through constant runs into the open spaces ahead of him.

    In deep build-up Brighton baited Arsenal in deliberately. Verbruggen put his foot on the ball while the centre-backs split and lengthened the pressing runs of their opponents. On paper that produced a 3v2 against Arsenal’s first line – except Hürzeler had no intention of playing through that overload on the ground. 25 of 40 goalkeeper passes were long, 62.5 per cent, and they went overwhelmingly to the right.

    The structure allowed for a long ball to the right flank, feeding into the 3-3 formation. This created opportunities to contest the second ball or flick on the aerial pass. Additionally, Vuskovic offered a short, low passing option as the free player.

    Sources indicate that there, Brighton consistently created a 3v3 – an intact structure for the second ball regardless of whether the first contact was won. That is exactly what separates it from an ordinary long ball: the action was not judged by the aerial duel but by the situation that followed it. Kostoulas dropping added to the disorganisation of Arsenal’s high line, because a centre-back had to decide whether to follow him between the lines or let him turn. After winning second balls Brighton played on at high speed and looked for an early shot or an early cross, even against a defensive overload – again the decision for tempo over the clean attack.

    Once again, the 3-3 structure on the right flank. Here, from open play.

    On the left Brighton worked through pinning rather than through length. Boscagli stepping inside dragged Saka into central areas and took him out of the wide zone Arsenal needed him in defensively, while De Cuyper dropped and offered the mid-range diagonal once the assignments had been pulled apart. The asymmetry was a personnel decision: the players for second balls were on the right, the players who could drag markers out of position on the left. Arsenal would have had to condense against one side and hand over assignments cleanly against the other.

    The team’s build-up play was asymmetrical, featuring a high, wide approach on the right contrasted with the left flank: Boscagli often played an inverted role—supplementing the existing diamond formation—which opened up space for de Cuyper. Meanwhile, Groß and Kostoulas occupied the players on Arsenal’s right defensive flank, enabling Brighton to find low-ball solutions against the press.

    With the ball in midfield there were two patterns. The first was the deliberate back pass to Verbruggen to pull Arsenal’s block out, followed by the same long-short structure as in deep build-up. The back pass was not a safety option here but the tool that created the space behind the pressing line in the first place.

    The second pattern worked through central and wide tension at high speed, supplemented by rotations within their own structure. Arsenal repeatedly failed to hand over their pressing assignments in a coordinated way against it – the same weakness Brighton had solved cleanly in their own press. In possession Brighton’s shape approached a 4-3-3: Chema Andrés as the deepest No. 6, Groß with freedom from the left half-space, Kadıoğlu pushing up early to support Gómez, Boscagli starting slightly deeper on the left.

    Recent findings suggest that the 1-0 by Groß in the 31st minute is the whole plan in one sequence. Brighton play back to the goalkeeper from midfield, go long, lose the first contact and win the second ball. After a phase of circulation the next attack meets a back line that has already been destabilised: Kostoulas drops, Arsenal’s midfield and Konsa step out, and Kostoulas lays the ball back against the direction of the pressure to Groß. Because Ayari runs in behind at the same time, Arsenal’s defenders drop – and Groß has the time for the shot from around 20 metres. In the build-up Brighton had used rotations to drag Guimarães over to the left.

    The opening goal stems from a positional attack. Kostoulas spots open space and makes a run into it. With a pass played across his standing leg, he feeds the ball to Groß in the space between the lines. As Groß takes a few quick touches and dribbles toward the defensive line, Gabriel and Calafiori drop back together, thereby opening up a shooting lane.

    According to recent reports, the 2-0 by Kostoulas shortly before half-time follows the same logic from the opposite direction. After a set piece of their own, Brighton clear an Arsenal counter and transition again immediately, 4v5 in Arsenal’s half, and once more the shot comes from distance while the centre-backs drop off.

    Much like the goal that made it 1–0, both defenders went to ground near the ball carrier, thereby opening up space for the goalscorer—this time arising from a transition situation.

    Sources indicate that both goals share the same cause: Arsenal’s centre-backs stepped out too late to press the man between the lines. React only when the shooting motion starts and you cannot get into the block from 20 to 25 metres. What is striking is that this passivity is the same one Arsenal showed in their own build-up – a side that does not leave its position to offer itself does not leave it to close down a shooter either.

    The 3-0 by Chema Andrés came from a corner: Groß delivered from the left, Brighton had created an overload at the far post and protected it with two blocks, and Chema rose completely unmarked to head in off the inside of the post.

    Two goals up, many sides would have defended deeper. Brighton came out with unchanged and at times higher pressing intensity, and the coordination was visibly drilled: marking assignments were swapped cleanly even in dynamic situations, and Arsenal’s structural adjustments were absorbed.

    Arsenal had managed a few organised possession phases in Brighton’s half in the first period; in the second it became harder. In those phases they built with a back three, Rice as the third centre-back, Ødegaard dropping alongside Guimarães and the full-backs occupying the half-spaces. Arteta reacted around the hour: Zubimendi and Merino for Timber and Guimarães, with Rice moving to right-back, followed shortly by Gyökeres and Eze for Ødegaard and Tzolis. There was no noticeable effect, because the problem did not lie in the shape but in the assignments in front of it.

    Sources indicate that there was also a layer that usually goes missing in analysis: Brighton used tactical fouls deliberately to stop Arsenal finding a rhythm. Arteta admitted afterwards that the game had been “very difficult to control”, pointing to lost first and second balls and to Brighton’s directness.

    In a recent development, arteta’s Arsenal being outplayed this clearly is rare. That it happened proactively and aggressively is rarer still – most sides who take something from Arsenal do it with a low block and efficiency. Hürzeler deliberately stepped back afterwards and praised his players’ courage, which gets to the heart of it: the plan only works if eleven players are willing to carry it through in every single sequence.

    It has been revealed that the interesting question is where the idea came from. Chelsea were a common opponent: Brighton had 74 per cent possession there and lost 3-4 against a counter-attacking side – control right down to the numbers, without return. Alonso’s Chelsea tried the opposite route against Arsenal, a deliberate surrender of control, also without success. The likely derivation lies between the two: neither give up control nor chase it, but generate the unsettled game state yourself and be prepared for it.

    Sources indicate that there is no reason for panic at Arsenal, but Arteta will need answers against a high press. The build-up was predictable for long stretches, and above all the direct option with pace in behind was missing as a threat. As long as that does not exist, a man-oriented press costs very little against this side.

    According to recent reports, for Brighton the open question is repeatability. Man-marking of this commitment, collective recovery runs with cover shadows and a touchline trap that requires everyone to trigger at once are hard to produce twice in an English week. Whether the proposal works was answered on this afternoon. How often it can be produced will decide the season.

    #38821. Rio, 1989: Chilean skullduggery, hidden razor blades and Brazilian flares

    Rio, 1989: Chilean skullduggery, hidden razor blades and Brazilian flares

    📅 07 Mar 2023 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the word “skullduggery” is defined as “underhanded or unscrupulous behaviour; trickery”.
    • It has been revealed that it should never be a surprise the lengths teams will go to in order to win.
    • To this day, Brazil hold the amazing record of having qualified for every World Cup finals tournament.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the word “skullduggery” is defined as “underhanded or unscrupulous behaviour; trickery”. It has been intertwined with football since time immemorial, exhibited in various degrees. It has been employed by the greats, not least Diego Maradona, and in recent times by compatriot Emiliano Martinez. Players have been banned from tournaments following drug tests and Serie A has been peppered by various instances of a dubious nature. Even the Brazilians are not exempt from employing it, as demonstrated by Rivaldo during the 2002 World Cup.

    It has been revealed that it should never be a surprise the lengths teams will go to in order to win. And yet it still does. Indeed, the story of Brazil’s 1989 World Cup qualifying campaign involved a classic example of the win-at-all-costs mentality. Sometimes truth is stranger than fiction.

    To this day, Brazil hold the amazing record of having qualified for every World Cup finals tournament. They have hosted the tournament twice, but on all other occasions they got through the CONMEBOL qualification process to reach the finals. To imagine them getting eliminated at that stage is almost too much to consider. After all, how do you stop a team like Brazil when you are a smaller South American nation?

    In the 1980s, Brazil enjoyed a generation of incredible talent, highlighted by the famous 1982 team containing the likes of Zico, Socrates, Falcao and Eder. Playing attacking football, they charmed the world before becoming unstuck against the Italians on an infamous night in Barcelona.

    It has been revealed that the loss brought about a period of introspection for the Selecao as they wrestled with balancing their natural attacking game with a more pragmatic European approach to avoid another 1982. Going into the 1986 World Cup, their style changed slightly, with more defensive steel added. They still had a team containing superb strikers such as Careca and Muller, but Zico was 33, Socrates was 32 and Falcao was the same. The 1982 generation was fading from the picture.

    Mexico 86 again saw Brazil eliminated by European opposition – this time in the shape of a France team that was also starting to see the end of a golden generation.

    It has been revealed that qualification for the 1990 World Cup saw Brazil up against Chile and Venezuela in a three-team round-robin. It was one of three CONMEBOL qualification groups from which the two top teams with the best records would automatically qualify for Italia 90 while the third top team would playoff against a side from the OFC section.

    Venezuela had a relatively weak squad and so the group would come down to Chile and Brazil; how they would perform against each other and what goal difference they could rack up against the Venezuelans.

    It has been revealed that both teams travelled to Caracas a week apart to start their campaigns, and both came away with comprehensive victories, Brazil 4-0 and Chile 3-1. Brazil’s victory included two goals from Bebeto and one from Romario – a deadly partnership that was beginning to click. That set the stage for the first meeting between the two, which took place in Santiago in August 1989. A win for either team would place them in pole position to win the group.

    It has been revealed that tension was high ahead of kick-off. With the game delayed by 15 minutes, the referee insisting on moving back photographers, Romario and defender Alejandro Hisis exchanged words. The striker took offence to something stated, Branco having to pull him away before things further.

    Within two minutes, the game erupted: Chile could have been down to ten men following a vicious knee-high tackle on Branco by midfielder Raul Ormeno. As Branco was led to the side of the pitch for treatment, a roar from the crowd drew attention to Romario. It appeared that he and Hisis were still feuding, and the camera revealed Romario being followed by three Chileans while Hisis lay on the ground.

    The referee revealed the PSV striker a straight red and Brazil faced 86 minutes a man short. If anyone wasn’t sure of what exactly had occurred, Romario cleared up the situation after the game: “I didn’t hit him that hard.”.

    Chile didn’t enjoy a one-man advantage for long. Fourteen minutes into the game Ormeno, who was clearly pumped up, lost the ball to Valdo and brought him down. Immediately realising the consequences, he tried desperately to persuade referee Diaz Palacio to keep his cards in his pocket. It was to no avail. A second yellow card was produced and the Chilean crowd howled as Ormeno had to be escorted off by four teammates. The first half was only a third of the way in.

    It has been revealed that scoreless at half-time, Brazil took the lead in the second half through an unfortunate own goal from Hugo Gonzalez. As the game stretched on, it appeared as if Brazil were going to leave Chile with a crucial away victory. But, with just nine minutes remaining, La Roja struck back through a bizarre goal from Ivo Basay.

    Sources indicate that brazilian goalkeeper Taffarel had the ball in his area when the referee suddenly decided that he had held it for too long and awarded an indirect free-kick to Chile just four yards from the goal. The quickest Chilean player to react was Jorge Aravena, who touched the ball to Basay to convert.

    Brazil were stunned. Chilean fans celebrated on the edge of the pitch, while the Brazilian technical staff went ballistic. There was confusion in every direction but, at the end of 90 minutes, the honours were even, little dividing the two countries in the standings. Brazil were marginally in front on goal difference.

    The following week saw O Selecao host Venezuela in Sao Paulo and dish out another lesson, running out 6-0 victors thanks to four goals from Careca, proving that Brazil still had three fearsome strikers to choose from. Seven days later, it was Chile’s turn to host Venezuela and, like the week before, Venezuela were again on the receiving end of a thrashing, this time going down 5-0.

    Only one game remained: Brazil against Chile in the Maracana on 3 September 1989. Both teams had two wins and a draw but Brazil’s goal difference was three better than Chile’s. If La Roja were going to eliminate their mighty neighbours and head to Italia 90, they needed to win in Rio. It would be a tough ask, but at least they were in a position where it was a possibility.

    Get an early goal and maybe the Brazilians would start to tense up in front of an expectant crowd. And let’s not forget that Brazil had suffered unexpected heartache at the Maracana before, losing the 1950 final to Uruguay. It was game on for that World Cup berth. But the Selecao had also never lost a World Cup qualification game in its history.

    It has been revealed that in front of a huge crowd of over 140,000, the two sides took to the pitch. Brazil would be without Romario – still suspended following the previous meeting’s sending-off – but with Careca and Bebeto upfront, they looked strong. Unfortunately for Chile, they would be without star striker Ivan Zamorano, who was unable to make it back from his Swiss side, Neuchatel Xamax, in time. The game was going to require an experienced referee, which it got in the shape of Argentine Juan Carlos Loustau.

    In a recent development, the last time Chile had beaten Brazil was a famous 4-0 win during the 1987 Copa America, and many of the team were in this side. Unsurprisingly, given the stakes, the early minutes were once again physical. Chilean left-back Hector Puebla left his studs on the knee of Mauro Galvao after just four minutes, although the referee didn’t blow for a foul. Then, just two minutes later, Bebeto tricked Puebla, who brought the Brazilian down and then appeared to stamp on his thigh. This time the referee saw fit to show Puebla a yellow card to calm the Chilean down.

    It has been revealed that the game continued with Brazil enjoying most of the possession but Chile remaining disciplined in defence. Although it was Chile who needed the win, they seemed focused on trying to reach half-time without conceding, rather than attempting to score. Brazil were creating chances, especially through Careca, but goalkeeper Roberto Rojas was equal to everything. Whenever Chile did venture into the Brazilian half, they were usually swiftly dispossessed.

    With Chile sitting deep, most of Brazil’s efforts were from distance – they were having difficulty penetrating the tight defence. Just before half-time, Branco hit a hard, swerving shot that Rojas did well to adjust to and save. And with that, the teams went into the break still scoreless.

    Brazil started the second half where they had left off previously – on the attack. And finally, four minutes in, they broke the deadlock. A defensive header from Branco fell to Dunga who played a quick ball forward to Bebeto. Spinning towards goal, he cleared one challenge before hitting a through ball to Careca. The Napoli star sidestepped Puebla before hitting a shot that, although partially saved by Rojas, went in. Brazil were 1-0 up and heading for Italia 90. Chile were facing elimination.

    For the following five minutes, Chile dominated as they tried desperately to get back into the tie. Brazil weathered the storm before taking control once again. It was impossible to see where Chile would get two goals from, which would mean committing men forward, leaving gaps for Bebeto and Careca to exploit. Then came the dramatic moment of the game.

    Industry observers note that on 68 minutes, Chile had possession of the ball in their own half through Astengo when a huge roar suddenly burst out from the crowd. TV cameras swivelled across to goalkeeper Rojas who lay in his penalty area while something flamed and smoked beside him. As the cameras lingered, it appeared as though a flare had been thrown by someone, Chilean players rushing to Rojas’ aid. As they understood what had happened, tempers began to rise. Patricio Yanez made several obscene gestures at the Brazilian fans.

    The Chileans motioned for a stretcher but, with none immediately forthcoming, took the initiative and carried their stricken goalkeeper off the field. The cameras showed blood running down the back of Rojas’ head as he was carried down the stairs into the tunnel, along with his teammates.

    According to recent reports, the stunned Brazilian players discussed what to do next with the referee, spending a further 20 minutes on the pitch awaiting the return of the Chileans. Eventually, the referee was forced to abandon the game, meaning that the likely solution would be a replay at a neutral venue. It appeared that Brazil had been just 22 minutes from Italy before their unruly fans ruined the day.

    Recent findings suggest that as mentioned, the TV cameras had swivelled to Rojas after the crowd noise drew attention to the incident. There was no footage of Rojas being hit by the flare, just his injured body writhing in agony on the floor. But one pitchside photographer, Paulo Teixeira, had seen the flare come onto the field – and something struck him as not quite right.

    Sources indicate that he could see Rojas bleeding from near his eye but was sure that the flare had landed many feet away from him. In a CNN interview, he recalled his immediate reaction: “I missed the shot and so did most of the photographers. But there was one guy by me, Ricardo Alfieri, a good friend, and I asked him, ‘Ricardo, did you capture the flare?’ He said, ‘Of course, about 4-5 shots.'”.

    Sources indicate that alfieri worked for a Japanese publication and so had to send his unprocessed film to them the next morning. Teixeira realised that he needed to move fast if his gut instinct was correct. Finding a local radio reporter, he convinced him to put Alfieri on air, who told listeners that he had shots that demonstrated the flare had not struck Rojas.

    Recent findings suggest that immediately after, the Brazilian football president, Ricardo Teixeira, came to the station and asked about the film. Together, they found a local lab and, dragging a poor technician out on a Sunday night, had her warm the lab up for the next four hours. Finally, they were able to process Alfieri’s film.

    Teixeira takes up the story again. “When the pictures came out, there were four clear shots – starting with the device flying and then landing one meter away from Rojas. [CBF president] Teixeira was so relieved.”.

    According to recent reports, the photos were published the next day by local news agency Globo while CBF President Teixeira flew to FIFA’s headquarters in Switzerland. There was clear evidence now that the flare had not directly injured Rojas. But if that was the case, what had caused the bleeding seen on his head?

    Two days on from the game, the medical report from the incident stated that there had been no burn marks on Rojas, just a cut on the left side of his forehead. Now back in Santiago, Rojas released a statement saying that he was shocked that people were doubting the nature of his injury.

    It has been revealed that rojas’ club side, Sao Paulo, were also publicly expressing doubts about keeping him on the books Finally, five days later, FIFA came to their decision: due to the lack of burn marks and Chile refusing to play on, the game was awarded to Brazil by a 2-0 margin. The Selecao had qualified for yet another World Cup.

    Recent findings suggest that but the mystery hadn’t been settled. Had a Brazilian thrown the firecracker? And how did the wound on the forehead arise? The first question was soon solved. It had been thrown by a Brazilian, a 24-year-old woman by the name of Rosenery Mello. After she was named in the press, she became a minor celebrity, leading to a cover pose in the November 1989 Brazilian edition of Playboy and the nickname “Maracana Rocket”.

    Recent findings suggest that the reason for her decision to appear on the cover? The CBF had fined her $12,000 for throwing the flare, while she was allegedly getting $40,000 for the cover.

    In a recent development, so now we knew where the flare came from that missed Rojas, but we still didn’t know what had caused the wound. The answer finally came out when Rojas was questioned further in the ensuing days.

    Recent findings suggest that he had concealed a razor blade in his glove ahead of the match in order to simulate injury should the need arise. Just think about that for a minute – a professional player had decided before a vital World Cup qualifier to have a blade ready with which to cut himself should he feel it was necessary.

    According to recent reports, incredibly, this wasn’t something Rojas had cooked up himself; both manager Orlando Aravena and team doctor Daniel Rodriguez were also involved. The whole scheme had, in fact, been concocted in the training camp to get the game abandoned at any sign of crowd trouble or player fighting.

    Sources indicate that unsurprisingly, Rojas was given a lifetime ban from the game, which was finally rescinded in 2001, allowing him to return to Sao Paulo as a goalkeeping coach and then manager. Chile were also barred from the 1994 World Cup qualification process, although more because of abandoning the game than the injury simulation.

    Industry observers note that both Aravena and Rodriguez, along with the president of the Chilean football federation, Sergio Stoppel, and the captain, Fernando Astengo, were punished by FIFA. Astengo has protested his innocence to this day, swearing he had no knowledge of the strategy.

    Recent findings suggest that this is not the only example over the years of what might be termed an “overreaction” to objects thrown from the crowd during a game. Of course, any such action by fans is deplorable and it is only natural that they should suffer sanctions But that has not prevented such actions sometimes being milked by the victims. The two best-known examples are probably the infamous Borussia Monchengladbach Coke can and the Celtic bottle.

    The Coke can incident occurred during the 1971/72 European Cup when Borussia Monchengladbach hosted Inter. With the Germans leading 2-1, Inter legend Roberto Boninsegna seemed to be hit on the head by an object, suddenly falling to the ground.

    According to recent reports, the object turned out to be a Coke can. Gladbach’s Gunter Netzer had his wits about him and disposed of the offending item, before Sandro Mazzola grabbed another from a fan and presented it to the referee. The upshot was that Gladbach won 7-1, but Inter managed to persuade UEFA to annul the game and replay it. Inter ended up proceeding to the final against Ajax.

    The second incident occurred when Celtic hosted Rapid Wien in the 1984/85 Cup Winners’ Cup. In a game that was already boiling over as Celtic took a 3-0 lead saw a penalty awarded to the Bhoys. As the Austrian players argued with the referee, a bottle was thrown onto the pitch from the Celtic crowd.

    Industry observers note that like the Brazilian flare, it missed everyone, but that didn’t stop Rapid’s Rudi Weinhofer from collapsing, holding his face before being taken off, his head heavily bandaged by the physio. Like Gladbach, Celtic were ordered to replay the game at a neutral venue – Old Trafford – and also were eliminated.

    Sources indicate that but both incidents were just feigning injury; they were not quite at the scale of concealing and then cutting yourself with a razor. And the truth is that, had it not been due to the quick thinking of a Brazilian photojournalist, Chile may have succeeded. Nowadays, such a rouse would be impossible given all the camera angles and mobile phone footage. But back then, it was a different ballgame.

    To paraphrase the Scooby Doo series, “Chile would have gotten away with it if it wasn’t for those meddling photographers.” It is a funny old game, indeed.

    #38820. Remembering the disaster of 1991/92, Bayern Munich’s worst season in modern history

    📅 06 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3129 w)

    Remembering the disaster of 1991/92, Bayern Munich’s worst season in modern history

    📅 06 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mention the words ‘Bayern Munich’ and what comes to mind?
    • It is a team that has won the European Cup six times and includes such notable alumni as Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Muller, Sepp Maier, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, Lothar Matthaus and Philipp Lahm.
    • But hard as it is to believe, they have endured ups and downs just like all teams – the difference being that a Bayern “down” is still normally what most other teams dream about.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mention the words ‘Bayern Munich’ and what comes to mind? A teutonic powerhouse? One of Europe’s elite? Serial winners? The Bavarians are, after all, a team that has won the Bundesliga 31 times – when the first was only 55 years ago.

    It is a team that has won the European Cup six times and includes such notable alumni as Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Muller, Sepp Maier, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, Lothar Matthaus and Philipp Lahm. It is a world-famous brand that stands for excellence. Bayern Munich equals trophies and success.

    But hard as it is to believe, they have endured ups and downs just like all teams – the difference being that a Bayern “down” is still normally what most other teams dream about.

    According to recent reports, but there is one season that will always live in infamy in Bayern history, a season during the 1990s when they were, frankly speaking, pretty terrible. Of course, terrible for Die Roten is relative – we are not talking about relegation here – but by their lofty standards, they turned into a mediocre team for 12 months. The season in question took place across 1991/92.

    Industry observers note that what’s more surprising is that there was no immediate sign beforehand of the slump to come. The 1986/87 campaign had seen an Udo Lattek-led Bayern win the Bundesliga, the manager whom Die Roten had dominated Europe under in the 1970s.

    In a recent development, that proved to be his final season before being replaced by Jupp Heynckes, who ironically had also replaced Lattek when he became Borussia Monchengladbach manager in 1979. While unable to replicate the Foals’ amazing 1970s success, Heynckes did lead them to fourth-place finishes in 1985 and 1986, followed by third place in 1987 along with a UEFA Cup semi-final, putting him on Bayern’s radar.

    Heynckes’ debut season (1987/88) saw Bayern fail to retain their title as an emergent Werder Bremen secured glory under the stewardship of Otto Rehhagel. With strikers Karl-Heinz Riedle and Frank Neubarth, and a defence that conceded just 22 goals in 34 games, Bremen finished four points ahead of second-place Bayern, having beaten them 3-1 in a key week 26 meeting. But normal service was soon resumed as Bayern lifted the Bundesliga the following year while also reaching the semi-finals of the UEFA Cup.

    The 1989/90 season saw Bayern even more dominant, again winning the Bundesliga by six points while this time reaching the semi-finals of the European Cup, before falling to the AC Milan of the three Dutch masters. Looking at the squad that season, it is notable that there were no world-renowned stars. The strike duo of Roland Wohlfarth and Alan McInally, while efficient, were hardly names that would’ve had Baresi, Maldini and co worried. But it was still enough to dominate Germany.

    It has been revealed that as such, the summer of 1990 saw Heynckes strengthen the squad by bringing in Stefan Effenberg, Brian Laudrup and Christian Ziege. Of these, the signing of Effenberg was by far the most interesting. A player who throughout his career would be no stranger to controversy, he was asked about why he had decided to join Bayern. Sporting his blonde mullet, he replied, “Because the other clubs are too stupid to win the Bundesliga.”.

    It was a surefire way to place a target on your back for the season, a comment sure to have been posted on opposing dressing room walls, including Kaiserslautern’s. An early season league game saw Bayern hammer Kaiserslautern 4-0 at the Olympiastadion before the season then developed into a battle between both teams for the title.

    Late March saw the advantage swing to Kaiserslautern as they defeated Bayern 2-1 at home courtesy of a late winner from Stefan Kuntz. That sparked a strong run from Die Roten and, with three matches to go, things were tight.

    Bayern then travelled to Bochum to face little-fancied Wattenscheid – a team that played in the tiny Lohrheidestadion and who Bayern had beaten 7-0 earlier in the season. To the shock of a watching nation, Wattenscheid held a 2-1 lead as the game entered the dying minutes. Then, with just three minutes left, the ever-reliable Wohlfarth scored to save Bayern’s blushes. Or so it seemed.

    Two minutes later, Thorsten Fink scored a shock winner for the team from Bochum to send 35,000 fans delirious – a defeat that opened the door for Kaiserslautern to claim their first Bundesliga title.

    Industry observers note that as if the defeat to Wattenscheid wasn’t painful enough, Bayern also suffered heartache in the European Cup. Once again, the semi-final curse raised its head, this time to Eastern European opposition rather than Italian. A strong team had emerged at Red Star Belgrade, who came to Munich and left with a 2-1 win in the first leg of their semi-final clash.

    Industry observers note that that left Bayern with a tough assignment in front of 80,000 rabid Red Star fans – flares burning in an intimidating atmosphere. But Die Roten rose to the task and the game was about to enter extra-time with Bayern 2-1 up when a freak own goal from captain Klaus Augenthaler in the last minute saw the Yugoslavs grab the all-important equaliser and move on to the final.

    Recent findings suggest that so as 1991/92 commenced, Bayern came off disappointment at the end of the preceding season but had still finished second in the league and narrowly missed on a European Cup final appearance. It was a season that many teams would die for.

    Industry observers note that the squad development continued as Heynckes brought in players such as Jan Wouters, Oliver Kreuzer, Thomas Berthold and two Brazilians, Mazinho and Bernardo. But balancing that was the retirement of long-serving stalwart Augenthaler. Still, Bayern fans were looking forward to reclaiming their position at the top of the league while perhaps claiming a UEFA Cup title.

    Industry observers note that the opening two league games saw an inauspicious start as Bayern drew at Werder Bremen before losing at home to Bundesliga fresh boys Hansa Rostock. They then travelled to Dusseldorf and came away with their first win, albeit only 1-0 thanks to a last-minute winner from Mazinho. Fans could start to relax ahead of a straightforward cup tie at home against minnows FC Homburg.

    Homburg is a small town in the Saarland region of Germany and their local team had been relatively obscure for most of its history. But, in 1986, they had reached the Promised Land of the Bundesliga for the first time. Their fans enjoyed two seasons at the top table before being relegated and then returning immediately. And so, travelling to Munich, the team was a second-tier outfit who typically played in front of 8,000 fans, even when in the Bundesliga.

    It has been revealed that only 9,000 bothered to trek to the Olympiastadion to watch the tie, resulting in a strange atmosphere within the vast bowl. It took 27 minutes but Bayern grabbed the lead through a backpost header from Mazinho. So far, so good. But Homburg emerged in the second half revitalised and had the cheek to equalise via a powerful shot from Rodolfo Cardoso.

    In a recent development, worse was to come for Bayern as, with just 13 minutes remaining, a loose ball fell to Homburg’s Matthias Baranowski, who gladly accepted the gift. This was not in the Bayern script and could not be permitted. Unsurprisingly, while Homburg fans were still rubbing their eyes, Mazinho scored again. Enough of this nonsense.

    And so the game went into extra-time when Bayern’s fitness would surely overwhelm the underdogs. But just five minutes in, Homburg’s Michael Kimmel jinked into the area and scored with a low shot. That pesky Homburg side just didn’t know when to lie down. And if that wasn’t bad enough, they then scored again four minutes later through Bernd Gries. Bayern were 4-2 down at home. That was how the game would end. A shocked Bayern had been eliminated in their first cup game by a lower division team in their own stadium.

    In a recent development, sometimes a cup defeat can be a blessing in disguise – at least now they could focus on the league and UEFA Cup. Maybe all was not lost yet.

    Their league form continued to fluctuate and, after nine matches, Bayern sat in seventh place as they prepared to commence their continental campaign. A relatively easy first-round draw saw them due to travel to Ireland for a first leg against Cork City. As Bayern fans researched where Cork was on the map, the players flew over.

    According to recent reports, cork City had only formed in 1984, following the bankruptcy of Cork United in 1982. A second-place league finish in the previous season had seen the part-timers earn their spot in the UEFA Cup. In front of just 4,000 fans, it was time for Bayern to forget about the Homburg embarrassment and start a successful UEFA Cup campaign.

    Dave Barry was a local who enjoyed a successful career with Cork County, playing Gaelic Football and winning two All-Ireland medals. But he also enjoyed regular football on the side and so turned out for Cork City as a midfielder. Ahead of the game, he had somehow come to the attention of Effenberg who, with his normal diplomacy, compared him to his grandfather.

    Recent findings suggest that picked for the game against Bayern, he wrote his name into Irish folklore when, after just 26 minutes, Cork stole the ball from the advancing Bayern defence and Barry found it at his feet. Charging forward, the balding midfielder turned inside one defender before rifling a shot home. The fans went ballistic.

    And so it stood until just before half-time when Effenberg finally brought parity to the score. Everyone then braced for the second-half whirlwind from Bayern, but it never occurred. The part-timers of Cork ended with a famous 1-1 draw against the German giants.

    Industry observers note that the second leg saw Bayern struggle once more. In fact, the Irish part-timers held out until the 71st minute before Bruno Labbadia finally spared Bayern’s blushes. A last-gasp penalty added a little more gloss, but at the final whistle, Die Roten had only just got over the line. Considering this and the Homburg result, all was most definitely not well in Bavaria.

    Three days later, Bayern travelled to Stuttgart and were hammered 4-1 – not by VfB but rather by Stuttgarter Kickers. It was finally too much to bear and, three days later, Bayern confirmed that they were parting organization with Heynckes.

    According to recent reports, the former striking great went on to enjoy a long and successful managerial career, overseeing teams in Spain, Portugal and Germany, including Real Madrid, Benfica, Schalke and his first love, Borussia Monchengladbach. He even returned to Bayern, becoming caretaker manager in 2009 after the firing of Jurgen Klinsmann before replacing Louis van Gaal in 2011 and leading them to a Champions League final defeat to Chelsea.

    Industry observers note that he then giuded Bayern to glory in 2013 by defeating Bundesliga rivals Borussia Dortmund in the final, making Heynckes just the fourth manager to win the competition with two different teams, Real Madrid being the other. One of the all-time greats, his dismissal after the Kickers defeat was later described by general manager Uli Hoeness as “the biggest mistake I ever made in my business life”.

    Industry observers note that A meeting was set up with club legend Franz Beckenbauer in Munich’s Sheraton Hotel to offer him the position as head coach. But he declined, stating prior commitments made it impossible. And therefore Bayern turned elsewhere – with a somewhat surprising result.

    It has been revealed that replacing Heynckes at the helm would be Danish legend Soren Lerby. A player who enjoyed three seasons with Bayern, during which they won two Bundesliga titles, he had only recently retired from playing at the age of 32. Taking the Bayern job represented his first step into management – a daunting task for experienced heads let alone a rookie. He didn’t even have the required coaching licence at the time of his appointment. It seemed a strange choice to most fans.

    Recent findings suggest that his tenure started off shakily as Bayern lost successive league games against Dortmund and VfB Stuttgart to drop to 14th in the 20-team league, just three places above the relegation spots. Next up for Lerby was, ironically, a trip back to Denmark as Bayern had drawn Boldklubben 1903 in the second round of the UEFA Cup. If Lerby thought it would be an enjoyable trip home, he was in for a major surprise.

    It has been revealed that not even the most hardcore Boldklubben fans can claim that their team had a grand history. They had won the league seven times, but four of those were before World War Two, while the most recent was back in 1976, before then merging with Kjobenhavns Boldklub in 1992 to form FC Copenhagen, who have enjoyed considerable success since.

    According to recent reports, they had only ever won two European ties and never made it past the second round. The visit of Bayern would represent one of the last games that Boldklubben would play before the merger. And what a game it was.

    In a recent development, over 14,000 fans packed into the Gentofte Stadion to see how their boys would fare against the German powerhouse. For 30 minutes the game was a stalemate, until Bayern snatched the lead through Mazinho. That lead lasted just five minutes before Michael Manniche tied the game. Tied going into the half-time break, there was little indication of the shockwave to come.

    Industry observers note that after 57 minutes, Boldklubben earned a penalty, which was duly dispatched by Danish star Ivan Nielsen. Four minutes later, the fans were in ecstasy as Kenneth Wegner made it 3-1. As the ground began to shake, the madness continued; just three minutes later, Manniche grabbed a second to put the Danes 4-1 up. The mighty Bayern had just conceded three goals in the space of seven minutes. And it wasn’t over yet.

    Brian Klaus added a fifth before Peter Uldbjerg made it 6-1. No-one could quite believe what they were witnessing. Markus Munch pulled back a last-minute consolation for Bayern but, as the final whistle sounded, all eyes turned to the scoreboard: Boldklubben 1903 6-2 Bayern Munich. Bayern’s season had just truly imploded.

    The return leg two weeks later saw Die Roten exit the competition with a whimper, winning just 1-0 through a late Mazinho goal. They had now been eliminated from the DFB-Pokal at home by a lower division side, from the UEFA Cup by Danish minnows and were sitting in 14th place in the league.

    In a recent development, given this start, it was no real surprise that Lerby was a dead man walking. He managed to stumble on until March when a 4-0 defeat away at Kaiserslautern saw Bayern, still stuck in the lower half of the table, finally wield the axe. It was to represent Lerby’s only stint in football management.

    It was time for a third manager that season as Hoeness turned to a much more experienced hire in Erich Ribbeck.

    Industry observers note that ribbeck had started his managerial career back in 1967 at Rot-Weiss Essen before managing Eintracht Frankfurt, Kaiserslautern, Borussia Dortmund and Bayer Leverkusen. His stats to date were at best mediocre – the only trophy he won during that period was the UEFA Cup with Bayer Leverkusen in 1988 – but he had Bundesliga experience and so was seen as the man who could right the listing ship.

    But Bayern by now were in a complete funk and so Ribbeck oversaw a final 11 league games in which they won five but lost as many as they stumbled over the finishing line, mired in mediocrity.

    Industry observers note that with the season over, Bayern sat in tenth, exactly mid-table. They had lost more games than they had won, including seven at home, and finished with a -2 goal difference. As usual, Wohlfarth was top scorer with 17, followed by Mazinho (12) and Effenberg (11). They had to sit back and watch while VfB Stuttgart, Dortmund and Frankfurt played out final-day drama to captivate the whole country.

    Industry observers note that all three teams sat on 50 points going into the final matchday and all three were playing away from home. Frankfurt had goal difference advantage and just needed to win, but shockingly lost to Hansa Rostock while having a clear penalty denied to them at 1-1.

    Dortmund won at Duisburg and were two minutes from being Bundesliga champions before Guido Buchwald wrote himself into Stuttgart legend with an 88th-minute winner at Leverkusen – despite being down to ten men following the sending-off of Matthias Sammer – earning Stuttgart the title on goal difference.

    That summer saw Bayern spend big. In came Thomas Helmer, Jorginho, Mehmet Scholl and, most newsworthy, the return of the prodigal son, Lothar Matthaus. Laudrup and Effenberg were moved on to Fiorentina to help fund the rebuild.

    Industry observers note that it worked: Bayern finished second in the Bundesliga, just a point behind champions Werder Bremen and with just five losses and a +29 goal difference. Ribbeck had successfully steadied the ship and would soon retire, replaced by Beckenbauer before a disastrous spell as Germany manager from 1998 to 2000. But Ribbeck also left with the unenviable stat of becoming the first and only manager of Bayern to be in charge for over 500 days without winning a single trophy.

    To this day, the 1991/92 season stands as a nadir for Bayern. Since the, Die Roten have only ever finished outside the top three twice, and have won 12 Bundesliga titles and three Champions Leagues. While 90s was often an inconsistent decade for Bayern – with players more often featured in the gossip pages rather than the sports pages, leading to the famous “FC Hollywood” nickname – nothing was as bad as 1991/92.

    In a recent development, bayern will always represent one of the elite European teams and are the gold standard against which many others measure themselves. Moreover, they have enjoyed success without the huge external financial backing that some other European sides have enjoyed.

    It has been argued by many that their recent dominance of German football has spoilt the Bundesliga as a spectacle, especially considering their ten successive. But it is refreshing to know that even teams like Bayern Munich can experience a season of woe. For that one year, they were actually human after all. And for that, VfB Stuttgart, Homborg, Cork City and Boldklubben will be eternally grateful.

    Industry News: Aspect analysis: Leipzig never found a trigger – LC

    📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 20.10.2026 in den Kategorien Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.
    • According to recent reports, A 6-1 reads like a game in which everything fell apart.
    • This aspect analysis therefore takes the goals rather than the game as its material and works back from there to the patterns.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 20.10.2026 in den Kategorien Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

    According to recent reports, A 6-1 reads like a game in which everything fell apart. Look at how the goals came about one by one and a different picture emerges: it was not six separate problems but two or three, which Bayern punished in seven variations. No pressure on the man in possession, marking problems in central areas, and a back line that did not work with the movements in front of it – that chain runs through practically every goal conceded.

    This aspect analysis therefore takes the goals rather than the game as its material and works back from there to the patterns.

    Bayern triggered very high throughout, stayed tight to their opponents and pushed through centrally without hesitation. Vandevoordt was pressed from Bayern’s right, with the clear intention of keeping him away from the left-hand build-up route and forcing the long ball. Leipzig’s front line of Nusa and Brajan Gruda repeatedly angled their runs deep against Nathaniel Brown and Konrad Laimer.

    Bayern had one extra central player dropping into midfield in this phase, usually Kimmich. Had Leipzig played short to the right, he could have pressed through onto Raum; in practice he stayed central and pushed through from there. That left Leipzig with the long ball, and it was ineffective: it produced almost no regains, so the enforced forward play brought neither relief nor territory.

    Going the other way, Leipzig got no access at all, and the reason was Bayern’s rotations. Kimmich dropped right, Pavlović left into a back three, with Upamecano holding a very wide position. Against this shifting three-man build-up Leipzig never found a trigger, because the assignments reset with every rotation – whoever was supposed to step out of midfield first had to work out who he was picking up. The handover of pressing duties out of central areas failed repeatedly.

    Industry observers note that in front of that, Bayern staggered their shape so that Leipzig’s compactness became the problem. Olise moved into the ten space at times, Nathaniel Brown operated in the half-lane and ran beyond from there, Luis Díaz stayed wide left. Saibari and Kane pinned several opponents centrally while regularly pulling out of the central lane. Because Leipzig pressed very narrow, this produced exactly what Bayern were looking for: once the opponent was committed near the ball, the switch followed, and on the now open side stood a one-on-one.

    That already builds the bridge to the goals. The isolated one-on-ones in which Luis Díaz got his three finishes were not individual moments but the product of this sequence of pinning and switching.

    Recent findings suggest that 1-0, Luis Díaz (12.) – The first goal already contains the full diagnosis. Kimmich receives centrally without any pressure and can turn out with an open body shape. Ahead of him Saibari and Kane occupy the central zone in front of the box, which forces Orban and Lukeba to step out – so far, the intended part. The full-backs, however, do not push up with that movement and stay too deep, while Raum’s position plays the runner onside. Klostermann stays outside and leaves the inside lane unsecured, and that is exactly where Luis Díaz starts from. Out of that unprotected lane Díaz runs into the back line and Kimmich chips the ball in behind. Not one bad decision, but four players whose decisions did not fit together.

    2-0, Aleksandar Pavlović (26.) – Same cause, different route. Kane drops deep and Leipzig do not shift across as a unit – the reactions highlighted it clearly: arms thrown up, gesturing, hands dropping again, the beginnings of frustration. Kane gets the free body shape, and with him the consequence is predictable: the long ball, high or flat. Because Leipzig are so narrow centrally, the ball flies straight through the entire zone in front of their back line. Luis Díaz moves actively into the passing lane to control it while Klostermann tries to get into his running line and does not make it – Díaz reaches the ball first. From the one-on-one he wins, Díaz dribbles centrally at Orban, which creates a four-against-three on the break. Díaz pins Orban and Lukeba centrally, Pavlović overlaps on the left after holding a high, left-leaning position all evening and threatening the back line. Two touches, left foot, finished away from the defender.

    Recent findings suggest that 3-0, Michael Olise (34.) – Here Bayern’s press shows itself at its clearest. From a Leipzig throw-in, the man-orientation is fully visible: consistent pushing through, clean handovers. A misplaced pass from Raum then cannot be defended, because neither the tracking nor the duelling is good enough to disturb the pass. Kane can open up half-way. Centrally, Olise comes inside from the wing, and Banzuzi and his partner fail to pick him up, letting him run through – against a player of that variability, an invitation to the key pass. Luis Díaz runs beyond and drags Orban with him, Klostermann is pinned wide by Saibari and can no longer get back into central areas. Olise finishes against the goalkeeper’s movement, across his standing leg into the far corner, catching Vandevoordt completely on the wrong foot.

    It has been revealed that 4-0, Luis Díaz (47.) – After a regain, Bayern switch swiftly to the far side and once diagonally through, putting Díaz in a one-on-one again. He holds the ball in the dribble, and Leipzig fail to solve the situation in three steps: the centre is not closed, Orban is too late stepping out, Klostermann does not get into the duel. That Vandevoordt leaves the far corner open is the final piece of an isolated one-on-one that should never have arisen.

    It has been revealed that 5-0, Harry Kane (53.) – Structurally the most interesting goal. Leipzig play a long ball without preparing it and react to the consequences contradictorily: the back line does not push up at all, while the midfield line and both forwards counterpress forwards. The ten space opens up enormously, the gaps between the lines become huge – and Olise is standing in that zone. One pass from Kim is enough to take six Leipzig players out of the game. Olise runs unopposed at the back line and lays it off to Díaz, who is in a one-on-one again; Brown joins for the two-against-one and shifts into the inside lane. Klostermann does not pick up his run from the deep half-space, and centrally Kane again drops into Orban’s blind side – a pattern that stood out across the whole game. The result is a two-against-one against the goalkeeper.

    6-0, Luis Díaz (69.) – From a set piece Bayern create a five-against-four out wide. Gnabry pins opponents and makes the space for Díaz, Orban again takes one significant step in the block and does not get into the duel. The same scene as the 4-0, only from a different phase of play – a sign that this is a behavioural pattern rather than a snapshot.

    Industry observers note that 6-1, Andrija Maksimović (90.+1) – Leipzig’s goal indicates in reverse what their own game had been missing. Bayern drop into a deeper block here, and Leipzig combine centrally before going wide. Gruda gets into a one-on-one against Brown, Upamecano steps across – but from above, with too wide a gap and without closing the centre. That opens the one-two, which Leipzig take immediately. Because the whole situation narrows onto that combination, the space behind it stays unoccupied, and Maksimović can take two touches on his left and finish unopposed.

    Sources indicate that the sequence of goals reads like a repetition. Five of Bayern’s six come from the same combination of no pressure on the ball centrally and a back line that does not manage the space behind it. Luis Díaz stands in an isolated one-on-one three times, Orban is twice too late with a step that is too big, Kane repeatedly drops into his blind side. Klostermann certainly did not have his best day – but it would be too easy to settle the bill with him. In the decisive scenes he faced situations that functioning protection in front of him should never have allowed to arise in the first place.

    Behind it all lies not an individual problem but a structural one: Leipzig pressed narrow and found no trigger against Bayern’s rotating back three. That very compactness made the switch of play the opponent’s most effective tool, and at the end of every switch stood a one-on-one that Leipzig lost. The scoreline is not the story – the story is that the same scene worked six times.

Secondo quanto riportato da Il Messaggero, Il tecnico ha ricevuto garanzie: nessuno partirà.     #38812. Access, Not Chances: How Como Took Manchester United Apart – LC
